en: The Treatise on the Nature of Enlightenment by Master Bodhidharma:
Now, as for the Way (*dharma*), it takes quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) as its essence; as for the practitioner, they take the departure from signs (*lakṣaṇa*) as their primary principle.

Thus, a sutra says: "Quiescent extinction is *bodhi*, because all signs are extinguished. A Buddha is one who is awakened (*buddha*). Humans possess an awakening mind; by attaining the path of *bodhi*, they become Buddhas. Therefore—
They are called Buddhas. A sutra says: "To be free from all marks is precisely what is called being a Buddha.
Thus we know that having marks is the mark of no-mark; it cannot be seen with the eyes, but can only be known through wisdom.

If one hears this Dharma and gives rise to even a single thought of faith, such a person has set forth upon the Mahāyāna and transcended the three realms. The three realms are greed, anger, and delusion. To turn back [from them]—
Greed, anger, and delusion are, [when transformed], precept, concentration, and wisdom; this is called transcending the three realms. Yet greed, anger, and delusion likewise lack any real nature;

they are spoken of only in reference to sentient beings. If one can reflect back upon oneself and clearly perceive that the nature of greed, anger, and delusion is itself the Buddha-nature, then apart from greed, anger, and delusion, there is no other Buddha-nature to be found. As a sutra says: "All Buddhas, from the very beginning, have always..."
Abiding within the three poisons, one nurtures the pure dharmas (*śukladharma*) and thereby accomplishes the "three poisons" of the World-Honored One—namely, greed, hatred, and delusion.
That which is called the Mahāyāna, the Supreme Vehicle, is the sphere of practice for all Bodhisattvas; there is nothing that it does not encompass.

There is also nothing to be mounted; though one mounts all day long, one has never mounted anything. This is the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). As the Sūtra says: "The absence of a vehicle is the Buddha-vehicle.

If a person knows that the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) are unreal and the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are merely provisional designations, and searches throughout their entire being for them only to find no fixed location, then it should be known that this person understands the Buddha’s words.
The Sūtra says: "The cave-dwelling of the five aggregates is called a meditation hall (*dhyānāyatana*); internal illumination opens [it]."
This is the gateway to the Mahāyāna; how could it not be clear? Not recollecting any phenomena is what is called meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
If one understands these words, then walking, standing, sitting, and reclining are all meditative concentration. To know that the mind is empty is called seeing the Buddha. Why is this?
Because the Buddhas of the ten directions all, by means of no-mind, do not perceive a mind; this is called seeing the Buddha. Abandoning the body...
To be without parsimony is called great giving (*mahādāna*). To be free from all movement and fixedness is called great seated meditation (*mahādhyāna*). Why is this?

Ordinary people are exclusively in a state of movement, while those of the Lesser Vehicle are exclusively in a state of fixedness. That which transcends the seated meditation of ordinary people and the Lesser Vehicle is called great seated meditation.
If one understands it in this way, all marks will be spontaneously liberated without being sought, and all ailments will be cured without being treated.
This is naturally so. All of these are the power of great meditative concentration (*samādhi*). For one who seeks the Dharma by means of the mind, it is delusion;

for one who does not seek the Dharma by means of the mind, it is awakening. Not clinging to words and letters is called liberation. Being unstained by the six sense objects is called protecting the Dharma.
Transcending birth and death is called leaving the home life. Not receiving further existence is called attaining the Way. Not giving rise to false conceptualization is called *nirvāṇa*. Not...
Abiding in ignorance is itself great wisdom. That which is free from afflictions is called *parinirvāṇa*. That which is free from the characteristics of mind is called the "other shore.
When one is deluded, there is this shore; when one awakens, there is no such thing as this shore. Why is this?
Because ordinary beings dwell perpetually on this shore, whereas those who have realized the Supreme Vehicle do not abide on this shore, nor do they abide on the other. Therefore, they are able to...
It is free from this shore and the other shore. If one perceives the other shore as distinct from this shore, such a person’s mind has not yet attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
What is called "sentient beings" refers to afflictions; what is called "bodhi" refers to awakening and understanding. These two are neither identical nor different;

they are merely separated by the presence of delusion or awakening. When in a state of delusion, there is a mundane world from which to emerge; when in a state of awakening, there is no mundane world from which to emerge. This is equality.
Within the Dharma, one does not perceive the ordinary person as distinct from the sage. A sutra states:
"The Dharma of equality is that which ordinary persons cannot enter and sages cannot practice. The Dharma of equality is practiced only by great Bodhisattvas and the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
To perceive birth as different from death, or movement as different from stillness, is called inequality. Not perceiving [these distinctions] is... [the Dharma of equality].
That afflictions (*kleśa*) are distinct from *nirvāṇa* is called equality. Why? Because afflictions and *nirvāṇa* are identical in their single nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Therefore, followers of the Hīnayāna falsely sever afflictions and falsely enter *nirvāṇa*, becoming obstructed by *nirvāṇa*.
The Bodhisattva, knowing that the nature of afflictions is empty, does not depart from emptiness; thus, he is ever in *nirvāṇa*. As for *nirvāṇa*:
Nirvāṇa is neither born nor does it perish; it transcends birth and death and transcends parinirvāṇa. When the mind is without coming or going, one enters nirvāṇa.
Know that nirvāṇa is precisely the empty mind. When the Buddhas enter nirvāṇa, they abide in a state free from false conceptualization.
When Bodhisattvas enter the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they abide in a state free from afflictions. As for the place of empty stillness—
This is precisely non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion. Attachment corresponds to the realm of desire; hatred corresponds to the realm of form;
and delusion corresponds to the formless realm. If a single thought-moment arises, one immediately enters the three realms; if a single thought-moment ceases, one immediately exits the three realms.

Thus we know that the arising and ceasing of the three realms, and the existence and non-existence of all phenomena, all depend upon the single mind. Generally speaking, what is called "a single phenomenon" is like a broken tile or stone.

Bamboo and wood are insentient things; yet if one knows that the mind is a mere provisional name and lacks any substantial reality, then one will know that one's own mind is likewise neither existent nor non-existent.
Why is this? Ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) invariably give rise to the mind, which is called "existence.
Those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) invariably extinguish the mind, which is called "non-existence. For Bodhisattvas and Buddhas, the mind has never arisen, nor...
The mind that has been extinguished is called the mind that is neither existent nor non-existent. This "neither existent nor non-existent mind" is termed the Middle Way.

Thus, one knows that if one holds to the mind while studying the Dharma, then both mind and Dharma are deluded; if one does not hold to the mind while studying the Dharma, then both mind and Dharma are awakened.
Those who are ordinary and deluded are deluded regarding awakening; those who have awakened are awakened regarding delusion. One of right view knows that the mind is empty and void.
One immediately transcends delusion and awakening; where there is neither delusion nor awakening, this is for the first time called right understanding and right view.
Form is not form by itself; it is form because of the mind. Mind is not mind by itself; it is mind because of form. Thus one knows that both form and mind arise and perish together.
That which exists exists within non-existence, and that which does not exist does not exist within existence; this is called true vision. As for true vision, there is nothing it does not encompass.
One sees, yet there is nothing seen. One sees filling the ten directions, yet this has never been seen before.
Why? Because there is nothing seen; because one sees the non-seeing; because one sees that which is not seeing. What ordinary people see is all called false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

If there is quiescent cessation and no seeing, only then is it called true seeing. When mind and object face each other, seeing arises between them. If the mind does not arise within, then externally—
When the object does not arise and both object and mind are pure, this is called true seeing. When one understands in this way, it is called right view.
Not seeing any phenomena is called attaining the Way; not understanding any phenomena is called understanding the Dharma. Why is this?
Because both seeing and not seeing are equally non-seeing, and both understanding and not understanding are equally non-understanding. This is the state of no-seeing.
To see is called true seeing; the understanding that is without [conceptual] understanding is called great understanding.

Now, as for right seeing, it does not merely see what is seen, but also sees what is unseen. As for true understanding, it does not merely understand what is understood, but also understands the absence of understanding.
Whatever there is of understanding is all called non-understanding; only when there is nothing to be understood is it first called right understanding. Understanding and...
Neither is understood; both are non-understanding. The Sūtra says: "Not relinquishing wisdom is called ignorance.
When one takes the mind to be empty, both understanding and non-understanding are true. When one takes the mind to be existent, both understanding and non-understanding are false.
If there is understanding, phenomena follow the person; if there is no understanding, the person follows phenomena. If phenomena follow the person, then what is not the Dharma becomes the Dharma.
If a person pursues the Dharma, then the Dharma becomes non-Dharma. If a person pursues the Dharma, then all dharmas are false.
If the Dharma pursues the person, then all dharmas are true. Therefore, the sage does not use the mind to seek the Dharma, nor does he use the Dharma to seek the mind;
he does not use the mind to seek the mind, nor does he use the Dharma to seek the Dharma. Thus, the mind does not—
Regarding the dharma of arising: the dharma does not give rise to the mind; since both mind and dharma are quiescent, one is therefore always in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

When the minds of sentient beings arise, the Buddha-dharma perishes; when the minds of sentient beings cease, the Buddha-dharma arises. When the mind arises, the true Dharma perishes; when the mind ceases, the true Dharma arises.
Knowing that all dharmas are each mutually unrelated is called attaining the Way; this is known as knowing the mind.
They do not belong to any phenomena. Such a person is always at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). When deluded, there is transgression; when awakened, there is no transgression. Why is this?
Because the nature of transgression is empty. If, while deluded, one perceives transgression as non-existent, then upon awakening, that very transgression is no longer a transgression.
Why is this? Because sin has no location. A sutra says: "All dharmas are without self-nature; do not doubt their true function. To doubt is to create sin. Why is this?
Sin arises from doubt and confusion. If one understands it in this way, the karmic offenses of previous lives will be extinguished.
When deluded, the six consciousnesses and the five aggregates are all afflictions and the phenomena of birth and death; when awakened, the six...
One realizes that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all *nirvāṇa* and that there is no dharma of birth and death.

A practitioner of the Way does not seek the Way externally. Why is this? Because one knows that the mind is the Way. When the mind is attained, there is no mind to be attained; when the Way is attained, there is no Way to be attained.
If one says that the Way is attained by taking the mind to seek it, such is called a false view. In delusion, there is a Buddha and there is a Dharma; in awakening—

There is neither Buddha nor Dharma. Why is this? Awakening itself is the Buddha-Dharma. Now, for one who cultivates the Way, the body perishes and the Way is accomplished, just as when a tree’s branch is broken.
This karmic retribution body is born; it is impermanent from moment to moment and possesses no fixed dharma.
One should simply practice according to every thought-moment. One must neither loathe birth-and-death nor crave birth-and-death, but rather, within every thought-moment—

If one does not give rise to deluded thoughts, then one will realize the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with residual substrate) while alive and enter the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena) at death.
When seeing forms with the eyes, one is not defiled by form; when hearing sounds with the ears, one is not defiled by sound—this is total liberation.
The eye does not cling to form, thus the eye is a gate to *dhyāna*; the ear does not cling to sound, thus the ear is a gate to *dhyāna*. To speak in general, seeing form is seeing [the truth].
The nature of form is non-attachment; it is eternally liberated. Those who perceive the marks of form are eternally bound.

One who is not bound by afflictions is what is called "liberated"; there is no other liberation apart from this. For one who skillfully contemplates form, form does not give rise to the mind, and the mind does not give rise to form;
thus, both form and mind are simultaneously pure. When there is no false conceptualization, the single mind is itself a Buddha-land.
When there is deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), a single mind is one hell. Sentient beings create deluded conceptualization;

because they produce mind from mind, they constantly dwell in hell. When Bodhisattvas observe deluded conceptualization, they do not produce mind from mind, and thus they constantly dwell in the Buddha-lands.
If one does not give rise to the mind from the mind, then thought after thought enters emptiness and every moment returns to stillness;
thus one goes from one Buddha-land to another Buddha-land. If one gives rise to the mind from the mind, then thought after thought is not still and every moment returns to movement;
thus one goes from one hell to another hell. If even a single thought arises, there are the two karmas of good and evil, and there are heavens and hells.
Hell. If not a single thought arises in the mind, then there are neither the two karmas of good and evil, nor are there heavens or hells.
Its essence is neither existent nor non-existent; it exists for the ordinary person but is absent for the sage.
Because the sage has no such [deluded] mind, his breast is empty and void, equal in measure to Heaven. All that follows below is the realization within the Great Way, and is not the Small Vehicle.
This is the realm of ordinary beings. When the mind attains nirvāṇa, one does not perceive nirvāṇa as something existing [apart from it].
Why is this? Because the mind is itself nirvāṇa. If one perceives nirvāṇa as being outside the mind, this is called holding a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
All afflictions (*kleśa*) are the seeds of the Tathāgata; wisdom is attained by means of afflictions. One may simply say that afflictions give rise to the Tathāgata.
Come! The afflictions from which the Path cannot be attained are the Tathāgata. Thus, the body and mind are the field; the afflictions are the seeds; and wisdom is the sprout.
The Tathāgata is likened to the grain. The Buddha is within the mind, just as fragrance is within the tree.
When the afflictions are exhausted, the Buddha emerges from the mind; when the decay is exhausted, the fragrance emerges from the tree. Then one knows the tree.
There is no fragrance outside; there is no Buddha outside the mind. If there were fragrance outside the tree, it would be another's fragrance.
If there were a Buddha outside the mind, he would be another Buddha. When the mind contains the three poisons, this is called a defiled and evil land.
When the mind is free from the three poisons, this is called a pure land. As the Sūtra says: "If one causes the land to be impure, filled with defilement and evil..."
That the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, should arise from within that [state] is impossible. That which is impure and defiled refers to ignorance and the three poisons;
the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, refer to the mind of pure awakening. There is no speech whatsoever that is not the Buddha-dharma.
If one can be without the object of what is spoken, yet speak of this Path all day long—if one can possess that [object]...
To say that one remains silent all day long is not the Way. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not rely on silence through speech, nor does he rely on speech through silence;
yet speech is never separate from silence. Those who realize this unity of speech and silence are all in *samādhi*. If one speaks at the appropriate time, even speech is liberation;
if one remains silent when the time is not right, even silence is bondage. Therefore, if speech is free from conceptual marks, speech itself is also [liberation].
This is called liberation. If silence were to cling to signs, that silence would itself be bondage. As for written characters, their fundamental nature is liberation;
characters cannot bring about bondage. Bondage has never, from the very beginning, been established by means of characters. In the Dharma, there is no high or low.
If one perceives high and low, it is not the Dharma. That which is not the Dharma serves as a raft; that which is the Dharma serves as a raft for people.
Those who board this raft immediately cross over from what is not the Dharma—this is the Dharma. According to worldly conventions, there are men and women, noble and humble;
yet speaking in terms of the Way, there are no men or women, noble or humble. It is for this reason that this heavenly maiden has realized the Way and remains unchanged.
Regarding the female form: Chanda understood the truth; how could he have been moved by a lowly designation? This is because it is not a matter of male or female, noble or base;
all arise from a single characteristic. For twelve years, the heavenly maiden sought the characteristics of a woman and found them utterly non-existent;

she then realized that for those same twelve years, she had likewise sought the characteristics of a man and found them non-existent. These "twelve years" refer to the twelve *āyatanas* (bases of cognition).
Furthermore, apart from the mind there is no Buddha, and apart from the Buddha there is no mind. This is just as there is no ice apart from water, and no water apart from ice.
When we speak of being "apart from the mind," it does not mean to distance oneself from the mind; rather, it means simply not to cling to the characteristics of the mind. As the Sūtra says:
Not perceiving marks is called seeing the Buddha; this is precisely the departure from the characteristics of the mind. Regarding the statement that apart from the Buddha there is no mind:
it means that the Buddha arises from the mind and the mind can give birth to the Buddha. Yet, although the Buddha arises from the mind, the mind has never given birth to the Buddha.
It is like a fish born from water, though the water does not give birth to the fish. If one wishes to observe the fish, before seeing the fish, one first sees [the water].
Water. Those who wish to contemplate the Buddha do not see the Buddha first, but first see the mind. This means that one who has already seen the fish forgets the water;
one who has already seen the Buddha forgets the mind. If one does not forget the mind, one is still deluded by the mind;
if one does not forget the water, one is still bewildered by the water. Sentient beings and bodhi are like ice and water. Thus it is said:
That which is scorched by the three poisons is called a sentient being; that which is purified by the three gates of liberation is called bodhi.
That which is frozen by the three winters is called ice; that which is melted by the three summers is called water. If one discards the ice...
There is no water distinct from this. If one were to discard sentient beings, there would be no bodhi distinct from them.
It is clearly known that the nature of ice is itself the nature of water, and the nature of water is itself the nature of ice. The nature of sentient beings is precisely the nature of bodhi.
Sentient beings and bodhi share a single nature, just as *wutou* and *fuzi* share the same root; they differ only in their timing.
Because they are deluded regarding different objects, there are two names: "sentient beings" and "bodhi. Therefore, when a snake transforms into a dragon, it does not change its scales;

when an ordinary person transforms into a sage, they do not change their face. It is simply that for one who knows the mind, wisdom shines within; for one who illuminates the body, precepts manifest without.

When true sentient beings deliver the Buddha, and the Buddha delivers sentient beings, this is called equality. As for "sentient beings delivering the Buddha," it refers to [the cessation of] afflictions...

From affliction arises awakening. When the Buddha delivers sentient beings, it is through awakening that afflictions are extinguished. Thus one knows that it is not the case that there are no afflictions, nor is it the case that there is no awakening.
One knows that without affliction there would be no way for awakening to arise, and without awakening there would be no way to extinguish affliction.
If the Buddha delivers sentient beings when they are deluded, then when they awaken, the sentient beings deliver the Buddha. Why is this? Because the Buddha...
It is not accomplished by itself; it is entirely due to the deliverance of sentient beings. All Buddhas take ignorance as their father and craving as their mother;
ignorance and craving are both alternative names for sentient beings. Sentient beings and ignorance are like the left palm and the right palm—there is no difference between them.
When deluded, one is on this shore; when awakened, one is on the other shore. If one knows the mind...
When emptiness is seen as devoid of marks, one is free from both delusion and awakening. Being free from both delusion and awakening, there is likewise no "other shore.
The Tathāgata is not on this shore, nor is he on the other shore, nor is he in the middle of the stream. Those in the middle of the stream are followers of the Hīnayāna;
those on this shore are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); and the other shore is *bodhi*. As for the Buddha’s three bodies, they are the *nirmāṇakāya*, the *saṃbhogakāya*, and the *dharmakāya*.

The *nirmāṇakāya* is also called the *saṃbhogakāya*. When sentient beings constantly perform wholesome deeds, it is the *nirmāṇakāya*; when they manifest the cultivation of wisdom, it is the *saṃbhogakāya*;

and when they manifest the realization of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is the *dharmakāya*. That which constantly manifests flying through the ten directions to provide salvation according to what is appropriate is the Buddha of the *nirmāṇakāya*.
If one cuts off delusions, this is the attainment of enlightenment on Mount Himavat; this is the Buddha of the *saṃbhogakāya*.
Without speech, without description, without action, and without attainment—serenely and eternally abiding—is the Dharma-body Buddha (*dharmakāya-buddha*).
If one discusses the ultimate principle, even a single Buddha does not exist; how then could there be three? These so-called "three bodies" are merely established according to human cognition.

Humans are categorized as superior, middling, or inferior. Those of inferior intelligence possess deluded profundity and the power of merit; they delusively perceive the Transformation-body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*). Those of middling intelligence... [text continues].

Those of inferior capacity falsely sever afflictions and falsely perceive the Reward Body Buddha (*saṃbhogakāya*). Those of superior intelligence falsely realize Bodhi and falsely perceive the Dharma Body Buddha (*dharmakāya*).
Those of the highest superior intelligence internally illumine perfect stillness; they realize that the mind is itself the Buddha and do not depend on the mind to attain Buddha-wisdom.
They know that the three bodies and all phenomena are neither graspable nor expressible. This is liberation.

Liberating the mind, one accomplishes the Great Way. As the Sūtra says: "The Buddha does not preach the Dharma; he does not deliver sentient beings; he does not realize Bodhi. This is what that means.
Sentient beings create karma, yet karma does not create sentient beings. One creates karma in this life and receives its retribution in a future life;
there is no time of escape from it. Only the Perfected Person, within this very body, does not create various karmas, and therefore does not receive [retribution].
Response: The Sūtra says, "If one does not create any karma, one will naturally attain the Way. How could this be empty talk? A person can create karma, but karma cannot create a person.
If a person creates karma, the karma arises together with the person; if a person does not create karma, the karma perishes together with the person.
Thus we know that karma is created by the person, and the person is born from karma. If a person does not create karma, then karma...
There is no way for a person to arise [without causes]. It is also like how a person can propagate the Way, but the Way cannot propagate the person.
The ordinary people of today often create karma yet falsely claim there is no retribution; how could they possibly avoid even a small measure of suffering?

If one uses the fact that [suffering] is slight to justify the preceding mind while creating the karma for the subsequent mind, when will there ever be liberation? If the preceding mind does not create [karma], then the subsequent mind will have no retribution.

Furthermore, regarding the establishment of false views and karmic retribution, a sutra states: "Though one believes that a Buddha exists, to say that the Buddha underwent ascetic practices is called a false view.
Though one believes that a Buddha exists, to say that the Buddha received retributions such as golden needles or parched grain is called incomplete faith;
this is called an icchantika. One who understands the teachings of the sages is called a sage; one who understands the teachings of ordinary people is called an ordinary person. However—
One who is able to abandon ordinary dharmas and proceed toward the noble dharmas transforms from an ordinary person into a sage.
Worldly fools merely desire to seek sages afar, yet they do not believe that the mind of wisdom and liberation constitutes a sage. As a sutra says: "Among those without wisdom..."
"Do not speak of this sutra. The sutra says: "As for the mind and the Dharma, those who lack wisdom do not believe that by understanding this mind and the Dharma one becomes a sage;
they merely desire to seek learning afar from external things, such as images of Buddhas in the void, light, fragrance, and color.
All such people fall into false views and lose their minds in madness. The sutra further says: "If one sees all marks as non-marks, then one truly sees."
The Tathāgata taught that the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates all arise from the single mind.
If the internal nature of the mind is pure, like empty space, one then transcends the eighty-four thousand afflictions within body and mind, which are the root of all illness.

Ordinary people experience grief at birth and sorrow at death; they are satiated when facing abundance and hungry when facing want—all these are termed great delusions. Therefore, the sages do not scheme for them.
Do not look ahead without considering what follows, nor harbor attachments to the present; let every thought return to the Way.
If you have not yet awakened to this great principle, you must immediately seek the wholesome paths of gods and humans, lest you lose both.
A Verse on Sitting Meditation at Night:
In the first watch, sit upright in the full lotus posture; With a serene spirit, silent illumination merges with the vast emptiness.
Since beginningless kalpas, there has been neither birth nor extinction; Why then seek to extinguish birth and extinction until nothing remains?
All phenomena are like illusions; their intrinsic nature is empty, so what need is there to remove them?
If one realizes that the nature of the mind is formless, it is serene and unmoving, its very suchness.
Second, further concentrating the spirit until it becomes luminously pure, one does not give rise to recollections or thoughts, becoming identical with true nature.
The myriad phenomena of the universe all return to emptiness; yet to further cling to the existence of emptiness remains a sickness.
All dharmas are fundamentally neither empty nor existent; it is only the deluded thoughts of ordinary beings that debate the false and the true.
If one can abide in the heart-mind without duality, who would say that the ordinary is not itself the sage?
At the third watch, the mind is pure and equal to space, Pervading the ten directions without anything it does not penetrate;

Mountains, rivers, stones, and walls cannot obstruct it. Within these worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, The fundamental nature of the world is the nature of True Suchness (Tathatā); It is neither existent nor non-existent, yet all is harmoniously integrated.
Not only can all Buddhas do so, but all classes of sentient beings are likewise the same;
In the fourth [state], there is neither extinction nor birth; Its measure is equal to empty space and the dharma-realm;
Without going or coming, without arising or ceasing; Neither existent nor non-existent, neither dark nor bright.
The Tathāgata’s vision does not give rise to any views; That which is nameless yet can be named is the true name of the Buddha.
Only those who have attained awakening can truly recognize it; Sentient beings who have not yet met it are like those born blind.
At the fifth watch, Prajñā illuminates the boundless; Without giving rise to a single thought, one traverses the three thousand worlds.
If you wish to see the equality of *tathatā*, be careful not to give rise to a conceptual mind;
this wondrous principle before your eyes is profound and subtle, beyond the measurement of the mind. Do not seek it out until you are utterly exhausted;
if you can remain without thought, that is the true seeking. Yet, if there is still seeking, you will not recognize it.
The Treatise on the Awakening of Nature by Master Bodhidharma (Concluded):
Verses on True Nature.
